content:
Meeting: Aurora Fintech — Security review (Demo Tenant / audit logs / retention / residency)
Recorded by Fireflies.ai
Date: Thu, Jan 16, 2025
Time: 10:00 AM - 10:44 AM PT
Duration: 44 min
Attendees: Avery Johnson, Markus Klein, Naomi Feldman, Kevin Osei, Dana Patel, Michael Chen, Sophie Martin, Laura Gomez

Summary (auto-generated)
- Aurora asked detailed questions on Redwood’s security posture for the standard sales demo tenant and for a potential evaluation.
- Topics included SOC 2 evidence, encryption, key management, audit logging, log retention, data residency (EU), and how prompts/outputs are handled.
- Redwood clarified that the demo tenant uses synthetic prompts, sanitized access, and controlled retention; and that Dedicated/Private modes support stricter isolation and customer-controlled retention.
- Agreed to follow up with SOC 2 package under NDA, an audit-log schema sample, and a technical deep dive for SIEM integration and residency constraints.

Topics
1) SOC 2 / compliance artifacts and security program overview
2) Data handling during demos (prompts, outputs, storage, human access)
3) Logging + audit logs (what is logged, redaction, access, export)
4) Retention defaults and configuration by deployment mode
5) Encryption in transit/at rest, KMS options
6) Data residency / regional routing and EU-only constraints
7) SSO/SAML, RBAC, SCIM, least privilege, break-glass access

Questions (captured)
- “Is the demo tenant covered by your SOC 2 Type II scope, and can you share the report?”
- “What exactly goes into your logs—do prompts/outputs show up anywhere?”
- “How long do you retain logs and application data by default, and can we set it to 0 or 7 days?”
- “Do you have audit logs that are customer-accessible and can they be sent to Splunk/Sentinel?”
- “Can you guarantee EU-only processing, including support staff access and backups?”

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send SOC 2 Type II report under NDA and a subprocessor list.
- Redwood to send an audit-log schema sample and guidance on SIEM integrations.
- Redwood to confirm demo tenant retention defaults and what can be configured for an Aurora evaluation tenant.
- Schedule follow-up technical deep dive (audit logs, residency, retention knobs).

---

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, looks like we’re all here. Dana, Michael, Sophie, Laura — thanks for making time. This is the security review specifically for the Redwood demo tenant and, you know, what an eval would look like.

[00:12] Dana Patel: Yep. Thanks. We saw the standard demo last week and it was good, but we have to do our normal security checklist before we let teams touch anything.

[00:21] Markus Klein: Totally. And just so you know, we’ve got Naomi on, she leads security and compliance requirements, and Kevin who handles audit logging and SIEM guidance.

[00:31] Naomi Feldman: Hi everyone.

[00:32] Kevin Osei: Hey.

[00:34] Sophie Martin: Hi.

[00:35] Laura Gomez: Hello.

[00:37] Avery Johnson: Great. Quick agenda: SOC2 and artifacts, logging/retention, data residency, and then we’ll leave 10 minutes at the end for next steps.

[00:48] Dana Patel: Works.

[00:50] Dana Patel: First question, is your demo tenant in scope for SOC 2? And can you share SOC 2 Type II.

[01:00] Naomi Feldman: The controls are the same control environment as our hosted platform, yes. We can share the SOC 2 Type II report under NDA. We also have a standard security package, like policies overview, pen test letter, and subprocessor list.

[01:15] Dana Patel: Okay. And when was the period end date? Like how current.

[01:20] Naomi Feldman: I’ll send the latest, but it’s current within the last 12 months. I don’t want to misstate the exact period end on the call; I’ll confirm in the follow-up.

[01:31] Sophie Martin: Is ISO 27001 in place or in progress?

[01:35] Naomi Feldman: In progress. SOC 2 Type II is the primary right now.

[01:41] Michael Chen: Cool. Next, data handling. In the demo you were typing prompts into the console. Where does that data go? Does it hit disk? Is it stored? Is it used for training?

[01:53] Markus Klein: Good question. For the standard demo tenant specifically, we only use synthetic prompts and canned scenarios. There’s no customer data in there, and the prompts are pre-baked for the demo scripts.

[02:05] Dana Patel: Sure, but in our eval, if our engineers paste data, what’s the default? Like is it logged.

[02:12] Naomi Feldman: Redwood does not use customer inputs or outputs to train foundation models. For logging: there are a couple layers.

[02:20] Kevin Osei: Yeah, so we separate “telemetry” — metrics like latency, token counts, error codes — from “content logging,” which would be prompt/response bodies. Content logging is not required for the platform to work.

[02:34] Dana Patel: Is content logging on by default?

[02:36] Kevin Osei: For most customers, no. By default we retain operational metadata. For some debugging flows, a customer can opt in to sampling content logs, but it’s a configuration and we recommend redaction.

[02:49] Michael Chen: When you say “metadata,” does that include full prompts? Sometimes vendors say metadata and it’s actually… content.

[02:57] Kevin Osei: Totally fair. Metadata in our default sense is request IDs, timestamps, model name/version, route, region, token counts, latency breakdown, and status codes. Not the body.

[03:10] Sophie Martin: And who has access to that? Like internally.

[03:13] Naomi Feldman: Access is role-based, least privilege. Support access is controlled. We also have an internal audit trail for access to production systems.

[03:23] Dana Patel: Do you have a “break glass” process? Like if there’s an incident.

[03:27] Naomi Feldman: Yes, and it’s logged and time-bounded.

[03:33] Laura Gomez: Sorry, from procurement, we also need the list of subprocessors and where data is stored.

[03:39] Avery Johnson: Yep, we’ll send subprocessor list. On storage location and residency, we can cover that now too.

[03:45] Dana Patel: Before residency: audit logs. We need customer-accessible audit logs, like who changed a route, who updated a key, who created an API token. Do you have that?

[03:56] Markus Klein: In the Console we have audit events for admin actions, yes.

[04:00] Kevin Osei: Let me be precise: we have audit events for control plane actions — login events, token creation and revocation, role changes, route changes, rollout changes, quota changes. Those are available in the Console and via export.

[04:16] Dana Patel: Export how? API? Or do we have to request it.

[04:20] Kevin Osei: There’s an API endpoint and also a periodic export option for enterprise setups. Most teams pipe it to Splunk or Sentinel; sometimes S3 then ingest.

[04:33] Michael Chen: Are these logs immutable? Like WORM.

[04:36] Kevin Osei: We can support immutability on the customer side by writing to their log destination. Internally they’re append-only and access controlled, but if you need strict WORM, we recommend export to your immutable store.

[04:51] Dana Patel: What about prompt and response redaction if content logging is enabled? Is there built-in regex redaction?

[04:58] Kevin Osei: We have a redaction layer for known fields when using structured output and tool calling; for arbitrary text, we generally recommend customers do not enable content logging, or if they do, they route it through their own redaction proxy. We can talk about patterns.

[05:15] Sophie Martin: Okay. Retention. How long do you keep logs by default? And can we set to… minimal.

[05:23] Naomi Feldman: Defaults differ by mode. For the demo tenant, we keep only what’s needed to operate and verify the demo, and we reset it. For a production hosted tenant, operational logs have a standard retention window; for Dedicated and Private, we can offer more control, including shorter retention, and in Private you can run with customer-managed storage.

[05:45] Dana Patel: I need numbers, though. Is it 30 days, 90 days, a year.

[05:51] Naomi Feldman: I don’t want to give you the wrong number live. We’ll provide the exact retention table in writing for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, including audit log retention. For many customers it’s 30-ish days for operational logs, but let me confirm.

[06:10] Michael Chen: For eval we’d want like 7 days max and ideally no content. And for some data, zero retention, like just transient.

[06:18] Markus Klein: That’s aligned with how we normally set up regulated evals. Also, we can configure so the app doesn’t store prompts/outputs. It’s mostly transient compute.

[06:28] Dana Patel: Do you cache? Like do you store the KV cache on disk.

[06:33] Markus Klein: The runtime uses KV cache in memory for performance. It’s not persisted as a product feature.

[06:40] Michael Chen: Okay.

[06:42] Dana Patel: Data residency. We’re EU-first. We can’t have prompts processed in the US for certain workflows.

[06:49] Avery Johnson: Understood. The question is: for the demo tenant, or for an evaluation tenant.

[06:54] Dana Patel: For evaluation and eventually prod. Demo tenant was okay because it was synthetic, but we don’t want to set the wrong precedent.

[07:02] Markus Klein: Redwood supports regional routing. So you can pin a route to an EU region, and if you need strict “no failover to US,” we can make that policy.

[07:13] Dana Patel: Can you guarantee that support personnel won’t access data outside EU? Also, backups.

[07:20] Naomi Feldman: For Hosted, there are limitations depending on support model and where the control plane runs; we can outline it. For Dedicated or Private, you get stronger guarantees: isolated capacity, stricter network boundaries, and you can control where data and logs live.

[07:37] Sophie Martin: Do you have an EU region today? Or is it “coming soon.”

[07:40] Avery Johnson: We do have EU regions available, yes. We’ll confirm which specific region aligns with your constraints.

[07:47] Michael Chen: Is the control plane also in EU? Or does it call back to US.

[07:52] Markus Klein: The data plane can be EU pinned; control plane depends on deployment mode. In Private (VPC) you can keep control plane private as well. In Hosted, some control plane services are centralized, but request processing can remain in-region.

[08:10] Dana Patel: That’s the key distinction. For us, “processing” includes logs, auth, and potentially model execution. We need a clear statement.

[08:18] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We can provide a written data flow diagram and a residency statement by deployment model. We don’t want ambiguity.

[08:29] Laura Gomez: Also, in vendor onboarding we need DPA terms, and whether you do cross-border transfers.

[08:35] Avery Johnson: We can route you to our standard DPA and SCCs where applicable.

[08:42] Dana Patel: Let’s talk about the demo tenant specifically. Who has access? How are credentials managed?

[08:48] Markus Klein: The demo tenant is restricted to Redwood internal users only. Prospects do not get direct access. In live demos, we share screen. For evaluation, we would spin up a separate tenant with your SSO if desired.

[09:03] Dana Patel: So the demo tenant is not something my team would log into.

[09:06] Avery Johnson: Correct.

[09:08] Michael Chen: During the demo I saw dashboards with token-level stuff. That implies you’re collecting token counts. That’s fine, but is any of that tied to user identity.

[09:18] Kevin Osei: In the demo environment it’s tied to internal Redwood demo roles. In a customer environment, you can configure API keys per app/team, so usage is attributed at the key or project level. For SSO, admin events are tied to identities for audit, yes.

[09:36] Sophie Martin: On RBAC, do you support granular roles? Like read-only security auditor.

[09:41] Markus Klein: Yes, we have RBAC roles including read-only views, and scoped permissions for routes, projects, keys.

[09:49] Dana Patel: SAML? SCIM?

[09:51] Naomi Feldman: SAML SSO is supported for enterprise. SCIM is supported for provisioning in enterprise tiers.

[10:02] Michael Chen: Encryption. TLS yes, but at rest — are you using KMS, and can we bring our own keys.

[10:09] Naomi Feldman: TLS in transit. At rest, we use envelope encryption with cloud KMS for hosted services. For Dedicated and Private, we can support customer-managed KMS keys depending on setup.

[10:24] Dana Patel: HSM required?

[10:26] Naomi Feldman: For some customers, we integrate with cloud HSM-backed KMS. For on-prem Private, it depends on your environment.

[10:36] Kevin Osei: And for audit logs, if you need them encrypted and shipped to your SIEM, we can do that.

[10:44] Dana Patel: Vulnerability management: do you do annual pen tests. Do we get a letter.

[10:49] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We can provide a pen test attestation letter in the security package.

[10:56] Sophie Martin: Incident response SLAs? Notification windows.

[11:01] Naomi Feldman: Covered in our standard terms. We’ll include that in the package and we can negotiate if needed.

[11:09] Michael Chen: For our evaluation, we would prefer either Dedicated or Private in a VPC. Can we do that without a long procurement.

[11:17] Avery Johnson: We can discuss. Usually we start hosted for speed, but for regulated fintech we often do a VPC-based private evaluation.

[11:28] Dana Patel: Another question: do you have human-in-the-loop review of prompts? Like do your engineers ever look at it.

[11:36] Naomi Feldman: Not by default. Support access is only when necessary for troubleshooting and is controlled. We can also set policies that restrict support access further in Dedicated/Private.

[11:50] Markus Klein: Also, for the demo tenant, there’s no customer content to view anyway.

[11:56] Dana Patel: Right.

[12:00] Michael Chen: Any egress from the environment? Like if the model calls tools.

[12:04] Markus Klein: Tool calling is supported; in your deployment you control tool endpoints. For hosted, you’d typically provide an HTTPS endpoint. For private, it can stay inside your VPC.

[12:18] Dana Patel: If tool outputs contain sensitive data, does Redwood store that.

[12:22] Kevin Osei: Same principle: we don’t need to store it; if you enable content logging, it could capture payloads, but default telemetry does not.

[12:33] Sophie Martin: Can you provide a list of what’s in “audit log events.” Like fields.

[12:38] Kevin Osei: Yes. I’ll send a schema sample: event type, actor, target resource, timestamp, source IP, request ID, outcome, and diff-style metadata for certain config changes.

[12:55] Dana Patel: Source IP is important.

[12:57] Kevin Osei: Yep.

[13:00] Laura Gomez: We also need to know if any of your support is offshore.

[13:06] Naomi Feldman: We can share the support access model and locations at a high level. For strict residency requirements, we’d recommend Private with customer-controlled access and logging.

[13:18] Dana Patel: This is helpful. Let me ask bluntly: if we choose Hosted, can you contractually commit to EU-only processing.

[13:27] Avery Johnson: It depends on the exact definition and the tier. We should take that as a follow-up with our legal/security. We don’t want to over-commit on a call.

[13:38] Naomi Feldman: +1. We’ll provide the written statement by mode.

[13:43] Michael Chen: Okay.

[13:45] Dana Patel: Another item: data deletion. If we send prompts, can we request deletion. Is there self-serve delete.

[13:53] Markus Klein: In hosted, you can delete keys and projects; for content, if it’s not stored, there’s nothing to delete. For any stored artifacts like logs, we can accommodate deletion requests per the DPA.

[14:10] Sophie Martin: Do you have a standard retention for audit logs that can’t be deleted.

[14:14] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs sometimes have minimum retention for security, but again, we’ll provide the exact policy and what’s configurable.

[14:24] Dana Patel: In our environment, we typically keep audit logs 1 year, but we want to control where. So exporting to our SIEM is fine.

[14:33] Kevin Osei: That’s exactly the pattern.

[14:36] Avery Johnson: Can I pause and make sure we’re tracking the key asks? SOC2 Type II, subprocessor list, data flow/residency statement, and audit log schema + SIEM export options.

[14:47] Dana Patel: Yes. And retention settings for an evaluation.

[14:50] Michael Chen: And control plane location detail.

[14:53] Sophie Martin: Plus incident notification details.

[14:56] Laura Gomez: DPA, SCCs.

[14:58] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[15:01] Markus Klein: Dana, can you clarify which workloads you’re evaluating? Like chat support vs internal docs. It affects whether EU-only is strict.

[15:10] Dana Patel: It’s initially internal analyst workflows, could be sensitive but not necessarily regulated data. But we have a blanket policy: EU data stays EU.

[15:21] Markus Klein: Understood.

[15:23] Michael Chen: We also have some latency requirements. In the demo you showed fallback routing. If EU capacity is constrained, does it fail over to US.

[15:32] Markus Klein: Only if you configure it. The fallback rules are policy-based. You can configure “same-region only” fallbacks, or “no fallback, just 503,” depending on your risk tolerance.

[15:48] Dana Patel: For security we’d prefer “no fallback” vs cross-border.

[15:52] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[15:55] Sophie Martin: One more: do you do customer-managed keys in hosted.

[15:59] Naomi Feldman: In certain enterprise configurations, yes, but it’s not universal. Dedicated and Private are better fits for strict CMK requirements.

[16:11] Dana Patel: Okay.

[16:13] (crosstalk)

[16:14] Laura Gomez: Sorry, can I ask about contract terms later. I just need the artifacts list.

[16:18] Avery Johnson: Yes, we’ll send a checklist.

[16:21] Kevin Osei: And I’ll include a short note on what’s in the demo dashboards — token counts, latency, error rates — and confirm it’s not content.

[16:29] Michael Chen: Good.

[16:31] Dana Patel: You mentioned “Console audit logs.” Is that separate from “platform logs.”

[16:36] Kevin Osei: Yeah, “audit logs” are like actions taken, “platform logs” are more like system events and metrics. Audit logs are what security teams care about.

[16:46] Dana Patel: Great.

[16:48] Naomi Feldman: Also, just to be clear: the demo tenant is internal-only. If your engineers want hands-on, we’d do an evaluation tenant with your controls.

[16:58] Dana Patel: Perfect.

[17:01] Avery Johnson: We’re at about 17 minutes. Anything else high priority.

[17:05] Sophie Martin: Do you have a trust center.

[17:08] Naomi Feldman: We have a trust page, yes, but detailed artifacts are shared under NDA.

[17:15] Michael Chen: Network security: do you support IP allowlisting.

[17:19] Markus Klein: Yes for enterprise. For Private in VPC, it’s your network.

[17:26] Dana Patel: MFA.

[17:27] Markus Klein: Yes.

[17:29] Kevin Osei: For API keys, you can rotate and set scopes.

[17:34] Dana Patel: Great.

[17:36] Avery Johnson: Okay, I propose next steps: we send the security package and then schedule a deep dive focusing on residency + audit export. Does next week work.

[17:46] Dana Patel: Yes. Tuesday or Wednesday.

[17:49] Avery Johnson: I’ll follow up with times.

[17:52] Markus Klein: Kevin, for the deep dive we can show a sample audit log export, like what it looks like.

[17:57] Kevin Osei: Yep.

[18:00] Dana Patel: Great.

[18:02] (The remainder of the call continues with minor clarifications on retention knobs, export frequency, and who from Aurora will join the SIEM deep dive; no additional major topics.)

[43:25] Avery Johnson: Alright, we’re at time. We’ll send: SOC2 under NDA, subprocessor list, DPA/SCC links, retention matrix, audit log schema, and set the follow-up.

[43:38] Dana Patel: Thanks.

[43:39] Michael Chen: Thanks all.

[43:40] Sophie Martin: Thank you.

[43:41] Laura Gomez: Thanks.

[43:43] Naomi Feldman: Thank you.

[43:44] Kevin Osei: Thanks.
